opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things that are really hard to get anywhere else, at least right now.

The first is compute. Physical AI, especially if you believe, as I do, that the path forward runs through large foundation models, is extremely compute-hungry. You're training vision-language-action models, you're running massive simulation, you're doing reinforcement learning at scale. A big company can give you access to that level of compute in a way that most startups or academic labs simply can't.

The second is talent density and breadth. Robotics isn't just one discipline. You need people who understand large models, people who understand control and hardware, people who understand perception, infrastructure, data pipelines. In a big company, you're sitting next to the folks building the frontier language and vision models. When we wanted to bring large-model capabilities into robots, the people who built those models were right there. That cross-pollination is incredibly valuable.

The third is patience, or the ability to take a long-term bet. Robotics has historically been a field where progress is slow and commercialization takes a long time. A startup lives on an eighteen-month runway, so there's constant pressure to ship a product, sometimes before the technology is ready. A big research organization can say: this is a ten-year problem, let's invest in the fundamentals. That freedom to work on the hard core problem, rather than a narrow application, matters a lot when the science itself isn't solved yet.

And finally, data and infrastructure. Physical-world data is the biggest bottleneck we have. You need fleets of robots, teleoperation systems, simulation infrastructure, tooling to collect and curate data. Building all of that from scratch is a huge undertaking, and a big company already has a lot of the engineering muscle to do it.

That said, I don't think it's one-size-fits-all. Big companies have their own challenges: they can be slower, there can be more process, and sometimes the robotics effort isn't the core business, so priorities can shift. Startups have real advantages in focus and speed, and we're seeing a lot of exciting ones right now. But for the stage we've been in, where the fundamental research questions are still open and the resources required are enormous, I felt a big company was the best place to push the frontier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says large companies provide compute and other resources that startups or academic labs generally cannot, and concludes that a big company was the best place to advance physical AI at this stage.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that robotics is an infrastructure problem before it's a research problem. If you want to do real work on AI in the physical world, you need three things at the same time: compute, data, and hardware. And each of those is expensive in a way that software AI isn't.

Take compute. The models we're training now for robot control aren't small. They're built on top of large vision-language foundations, and fine-tuning or co-training them on robot data takes the same class of TPU or GPU clusters that language teams use. A startup can rent that, but it burns through runway fast. Inside a big company, that capacity exists already, and the marginal cost of letting a robotics team use it is manageable.

Then data. In language, the internet is your dataset. In robotics, there is no internet of robot experience. You have to go generate it. That means fleets of physical robots, operators, teleoperation rigs, simulation at scale, and the engineering to make all of that reliable. We ran dozens of robots collecting data for years before some of the results people now cite were possible. That's a sustained capital commitment, and a big company can make it without needing a product in year one.

The third piece is patience, honestly. Physical AI has a longer horizon than most investors are comfortable with. Big companies have their own pressures, but they can afford to say, this is a ten-year bet, and keep funding it through the periods where the demos aren't impressive yet.

There's also the people side. The best robotics work right now is interdisciplinary. You need people who understand reinforcement learning, people who understand foundation models, hardware engineers, control theorists, and people who care about safety. At a large lab, those people already exist down the hall. The vision-language model researchers I collaborate with weren't hired for robotics, but when we started asking whether their models could reason about physical scenes, they were right there, and that's how projects like RT-2 came together.

I don't want to say startups can't do it. Some are doing very impressive things, and the energy there is real. But my view is that if you want to push the frontier of what's possible, rather than build one product on top of what's already known, the big company environment gives you the resources to take the harder, slower path. That's what drew me to it, and it's still what keeps me there.

r001.rationale: The response argues that large models make physical-world AI resource-intensive and that big companies can provide the compute, robot data, hardware, and long-term funding needed to push the frontier—presenting them as especially viable settings.

astra-6.text:
I think AI in the physical world requires a combination of resources that’s hard to bring together. You need strong AI researchers, but you also need people who understand hardware, control, and how to make a system reliable. A big company can bring those people together and provide the compute and infrastructure to support them.

The other part is the time horizon. With robotics, you have to build things, test them in the real world, discover what fails, and try again. That can be a slow process. Having the support to keep working through those cycles is a big advantage. For me, the appeal is being able to pursue ambitious research while also having a path to turn it into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response explains why a big company is advantageous for physical-world AI, citing people, compute, infrastructure, and time for testing. It does not communicate that large companies are among the few viable settings or connect that claim to the era of large models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big company can be a very good place for this because AI in the physical world requires more than a good algorithm. You need hardware, infrastructure, compute, and people with different kinds of expertise working together. You also need the patience to iterate: build a system, test it in the real world, understand why it fails, and improve it.

A big company can bring those resources together and support that longer research cycle. And it can connect research to practical applications. For me, that’s exciting—the opportunity to explore fundamental questions while also working toward systems that can do something useful in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says a big company is a good place because it can provide resources and support longer research cycles, but it does not argue that large companies are among the few viable settings or connect that claim to the era of large models.
